opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the difference is subtler than people assume. Math has this beautiful property where you have a formal ground truth. If you're working in something like Lean, a proof either checks or it doesn't. That gives you a very clean reward signal, and it's part of why you've seen such rapid progress there: you can generate, verify, and iterate in a tight loop without a human in it.

Physics doesn't really work that way. The ultimate arbiter in physics isn't a proof checker; it's nature. And a lot of what physicists actually do day to day lives in between rigor and experiment. We make approximations, we drop terms we think are small, we use effective theories that we know are wrong at some scale but are extremely useful at the scale we care about. A good physicist has taste about which approximations are legitimate and which ones are going to bite you. That's very hard to formalize, and if you tried to force everything into a fully rigorous framework, you'd actually lose a lot of what makes physics productive.

So when I think about helping physicists with AI, the system needs something closer to physical intuition. It needs to know when a calculation is "good enough," when a result smells wrong because it violates a symmetry or has the wrong dimensions or blows up in a limit where it shouldn't. Those sanity checks are a kind of verification, but they're soft, and they're heuristic.

That said, I don't think the two are totally separate. Many of the reasoning skills overlap: long chains of careful calculation, keeping track of what you've assumed, backtracking when something doesn't work. And there's a lot of mathematics inside physics where formal tools could absolutely help. But the frontier of physics research is really about asking the right question and building the right model, and that's where I think the interesting, harder problem is. In some sense, math gives AI a sandbox with perfect rules, and physics asks it to go out into the messy world and figure out which rules matter.

r001.rationale: The response says approximations and effective theories can be useful and productive, but does not say that physicists’ informal reasoning is highly explanatory.

r002.rationale: It identifies asking the right question and building the right model as the frontier of physics research, distinguishing this from work within formal rules.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that AI training data should capture physicists’ informal research conversations.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that they're almost different problems, even though from the outside they look like the same thing—"AI does hard technical work."

Math proofs are, in a sense, the cleanest possible target. You have a formal statement, you have a verifier, and the question is binary: did you prove it or not? That's why it's been such a productive domain for AI—you can scale up search, you can get a clean reward signal, you can run in Lean or whatever and know when you're done. The model doesn't need taste, really, in the sense of knowing which problems matter. It just needs to be good at the game.

Physics is different because the hard part usually isn't the derivation. The hard part is figuring out what the right question is, what the right approximation is, what to throw away. When a physicist is stuck, it's rarely because they can't do the integral. It's because they don't know which effective description captures the thing they care about, or they've got the wrong variables. There's no verifier for that. The "proof" is nature, and you don't get to query it quickly.

So when I think about AI helping physicists, I think less about an oracle that spits out the answer and more about something closer to a very good collaborator—something that can hold a lot of the literature in its head, try ten half-baked ideas in an afternoon, do the tedious calculation you'd otherwise put off for a week, and push back when your intuition is off. The value is in compressing the loop, not in replacing judgment.

The other thing I'd say is that physics and the current systems share a kind of culture. Physicists are comfortable being wrong in a controlled way—you make a crude model, you see what it predicts, you refine. That's a very natural mode for working with a model that's powerful but not perfectly reliable. You're not asking it to be right; you're asking it to be useful enough that the human can do the error correction.

And frankly, I think the lessons flow both ways. A lot of what we understand about these systems—scaling laws, how they generalize, what's going on inside—has come from people with a physics sensibility treating the networks as physical objects to be studied. So the question of "AI for physics" and "physics for AI" aren't really separable for me.

r001.rationale: The response describes physicists using crude models and refining them, but does not say that their informal reasoning is highly explanatory.

r002.rationale: It identifies choosing the right question, approximation, effective description, and variables as central challenges, contrasting them with doing the derivation.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that physics AI training data should capture informal research conversations.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is that in mathematics, once you’ve specified the statement and the rules, there’s a very crisp notion of success: you have a proof, and you can check it. Finding that proof can be extraordinarily hard, but verification is relatively well defined.

In physics, figuring out what the problem should be is often a huge part of the work. Which features of a system matter? What can you neglect? What approximation gives you some insight? You can do a calculation perfectly and still have chosen a model that doesn’t describe the phenomenon you care about.

So helping physicists requires more than getting the algebra right. You want a system that can move between physical intuition, mathematical models, numerical experiments, and actual observations. Sometimes a useful answer is an approximate answer that reveals why something happens, rather than an exact expression that’s difficult to interpret.

That makes the collaboration especially interesting. The AI might help you explore possible models or test a conjecture, but the standard ultimately comes from nature. A proof tells you what follows from your assumptions; physics also asks whether those were the right assumptions in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says physical intuition and approximate answers can reveal why something happens, but it does not characterize physicists’ informal reasoning as explanatory.

r002.rationale: It identifies determining which features matter, what to neglect, and which model describes the phenomenon as a major part of physics work.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that physics AI training data should capture informal research conversations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difference is what counts as success. In mathematics, you can state a problem precisely and, if you produce a formal proof, check whether it’s correct. That gives you a very clean feedback signal.

In physics, figuring out the right question is often a big part of the work. You’re choosing which assumptions to make, which effects to neglect, and what approximation might reveal the underlying mechanism. A calculation can be perfectly correct and still fail to describe nature.

So helping physicists means working across that whole process: suggesting models, doing calculations, comparing predictions with data, and helping us understand why something happens. Proving things can be part of that, but ultimately the arbiter is experiment. I’d want an AI collaborator that helps us develop physical intuition as well as get an answer.

r001.rationale: The response mentions developing physical intuition and understanding mechanisms, but does not say that informal reasoning can be highly explanatory.

r002.rationale: It says that figuring out the right question and choosing assumptions, neglected effects, and approximations are central to physics, distinguishing this from solving a precisely stated problem.
